Article Title: 'Bas lage rhna hai': Back in rhythm, Mukesh Kumar pushes for India comeback | EXCLUSIVE
Article Text:
Mukesh Kumar celebrates a wicket during the Duleep Trophy. (PTI)

NEW DELHI: The last time Mukesh Kumar played for India, he claimed a four-wicket haul against Zimbabwe in Harare. Since then, he has been out of the national setup. More than two years later, the Bengal pacer is back on the selectors’ radar after being picked in the India A squad for the New Zealand tour.What can a cricketer do when they have played all three formats for India and are then suddenly left out in the cold? "Bas lage rhna hai (All we can do is keep pushing)," Mukesh tells TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.Mukesh, who will turn 33 in three days, is getting ready to play his sixth first-class game in less than two months. He picked up 12 wickets in East Zone's title triumph in the Duleep Trophy, then went on to play a county match for Nottinghamshire, before returning to pick up eight wickets in the Irani Cup, helping Rest of India lift the trophy. Now, from Sunday, he will be playing for Bengal against Delhi in their Ranji Trophy opener before taking a flight to New Zealand.The seamer, who struggled with a calf injury last season, admits he is at his best in terms of fitness and says he has found his rhythm."As a rhythm bowler, I need to play regularly to get into my groove, particularly in red-ball cricket. The longer I play through a season, the better my rhythm becomes. That did not happen last year because of the injury," he said."I had an injury last year and did not get to play much. I played only three Ranji Trophy matches, two or three Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy matches and five Vijay Hazare Trophy matches.This year, however, I have already been part of teams that won the Duleep Trophy and the Irani Cup. I am enjoying my cricket, my body is getting into a rhythm, and I feel I have prepared well," he added.One thing Mukesh is enjoying most about this season is the way the ball is leaving his hand. What has worked well for him is his upright seam. He feels his wrist is firmly cocked at the point of delivery, and his slightly split fingers come down so straight that the seam invariably comes out bolt upright."My strength is my seam position. I am not someone who relies heavily on swing. Whatever the ball is, whether it is an SG, Duke or Kookaburra, I try to land it on the seam," he said."My rhythm was slightly off in the first innings (of the Duleep Trophy). I could not quite understand what was happening, although the pitch was offering plenty of assistance on the first day. Even when my rhythm was not at its best, I managed to trouble the batters. I started finding my rhythm towards the end of the first innings, and it carried into the second innings. Once that happened, you saw the difference."Mukesh also candidly admits that most of his wickets this season have come with the SG ball. Of the 22 wickets he has taken this season, 21 have come in India with the SG ball. He picked up a solitary wicket in the one county match he played for Nottinghamshire. Mukesh has experience of bowling in different conditions, but this time around, he is doing his homework before landing in New Zealand.In the Bengal team, he shares the dressing room with Mohammed Shami and Akash Deep, but he has also reached out to Sourav Ganguly."I have played in Australia, Bangladesh and South Africa, so I have experience of bowling in different conditions," he said."I speak to Ranadeb Bose most often. I also talk to Laxmi Ratan Shukla. Recently, I had a long chat with Mohammed Shami as well. He has shared his experience of bowling in New Zealand and has advised me on things I can do differently."I have also met Sourav sir. He was one of India's best captains. He has shared details about the conditions in New Zealand. I enjoyed exchanging ideas with him," said Mukesh.Mukesh knows he is not getting any younger. He has the skill set but for fast bowlers, that's not always enough. A three-point plan was drawn for the off-season and the hard yards are paying off."The first thing I worked a lot on was my fitness. I have also worked extensively on my line and length. Lastly, I have added a few yards to my pace. These were the three areas I focused on, and the improvement was visible in my bowling during the Duleep Trophy and Irani Cup," he said.Mukesh also talks about the insecurity that creeps into a fast bowler's mind when he gets injured, as rehabilitation can be a long and frustrating process. He also explains the changes a bowler needs to make to regain full fitness."A fast bowler has to be careful about his diet. You need to avoid too much oily and spicy food. Getting adequate sleep and maintaining good habits are key as well. Mental peace is another important aspect. If you keep worrying about things, you will not sleep properly and may end up staying awake all night. You need to eat well, sleep well, follow good habits and keep up with your rehabilitation. You must also follow the instructions of your trainers and physiotherapists."At times, the mind can become frustrated when you are injured. Cricket is happening all over the world, and you are lying in bed, unable to play. You see other players representing India and wonder when you will return. I am very grateful to God that I have such a supportive family. Whatever happens at home, my family ensures that it does not affect me. My mother, in particular, makes sure that I do not have to worry about anything. Now I have my wife as well, so that support system is important," he said.For fast bowlers, the packed cricket calendar leaves little room to breathe. The IPL is followed by state leagues and then a packed domestic season featuring tournaments such as the Duleep Trophy, Irani Cup and Ranji Trophy, along with the white-ball competitions. With matches coming thick and fast, managing workloads becomes crucial, particularly for bowlers whose bodies endure immense physical stress. Injuries can derail careers, making it essential to recognise the warning signs.So, how does a fast bowler know when he is pushing his body too far?"Body hamesha 80% hi rehta hai, 20% niggle toh rehta hi hai (A fast bowler can never be 100% fit. There will always be some niggle or the other)," he said with a laugh."Before an injury happens, the body gives you signals. It is almost as if God is telling you not to push yourself any further because something could go wrong. The body works in a similar way. If you push beyond your limits, you may end up getting injured. If you understand your body and recognise those warning signs, you can ease off and ask for rest when necessary. For example, if you feel tightness or stiffness, you should communicate that to the team management and explain that you might need a break from the next match.Ultimately, it also depends on what the management wants and how it assesses the situation."You have to recognise when your workload is becoming excessive. If there is a tight match, you naturally want to give everything you have. You feel that whatever happens afterwards can be dealt with later. But you cannot approach every match that way. You have to understand when your body needs rest. If you do not, you could end up paying a heavy price," he further explained.A workhorse in domestic cricket, Mukesh has earned recognition for his performances and is now back in contention for a place in the national setup. With a new challenge awaiting him in New Zealand, the Bengal pacer knows that every opportunity counts. After more than two years on the sidelines, he is determined to keep pushing and make his way back into the Indian dressing room.
Article Summary: Mukesh Kumar picked in India A squad for New Zealand tour. Last time he played for India, he claimed a four-wicket haul against Zimbabwe in Harare. Bengal pacer is getting ready to play his sixth first-class game in less than two months.

Article Title: ‘I was a daughter of Himachal’: Ritu Negi’s heartbreak after home state drops Asian Games gold medallist from Rs 1 crore reward list
Article Text:
Indian women's Kabaddi player Ritu Negi. (ANI Photo)

‘Why is Himachal Pradesh behaving this way at this stage of my career?’

India women's kabaddi team after winning the Asian Games gold medal in Japan.

Her father asks: Does a daughter stop belonging to her state after marriage?

Why three kabaddi players were awarded Rs 1 crore each

Government promises to review the decision

Another gold medal, but a different kind of disappointment

Former India captain Ritu Negi has represented the country at three consecutive Asian Games, won two gold medals and a silver, and led the women's kabaddi team to the top of the podium at the 2023 edition in Hangzhou. Yet, after being part of India's gold-medal-winning squad again at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the Arjuna Awardee has found herself at the centre of an unexpected controversy in her home state of Himachal Pradesh.Negi's name was missing from the state's list of athletes announced for a cash reward of Rs 1 crore following India's women's kabaddi triumph in Japan. The decision has left the veteran player disappointed and raised questions about whether an accomplished sportsperson should lose recognition from her home state simply because she is married in another state.Negi hails from the Shillai region of Sirmaur district but is married in Panipat, Haryana. The omission has been particularly difficult to understand because she received a cash reward from Himachal Pradesh after India's women's kabaddi team won gold at the 2023 Asian Games, when she was the captain.This time, however, her name was left out while three other players from the state were included in the reward list."Until a week ago, I was a daughter of Himachal and the CM shared a congratulatory message on Facebook, while former CM Jairam Thakur and Member of Parliament Anurag Thakur had called to congratulate me," Negi told the media while expressing her displeasure."I simply cannot understand what changed so suddenly two days ago."The decision to exclude Negi has struck a particularly sensitive chord because of her long association with Indian kabaddi and her contribution to the state's sporting reputation.The veteran has represented India at three consecutive Asian Games, winning two gold medals and a silver. She captained the women's team to gold at Hangzhou in 2023 and remained part of the squad that successfully defended the title in Japan.India edged past Iran 37-34 in a tense final at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, holding on to its advantage in the closing stages to secure another Asian Games gold.The achievement should have been another moment of pride for the player and her home state. Instead, the omission from the reward list has left Negi questioning the recognition being extended to her.She pointed out that although she is employed by Indian Railways , she has consistently represented Himachal Pradesh, rather than Haryana, in domestic competitions."Why Himachal Pradesh is behaving in such a way at this stage of my career?" she asked.For Negi, the issue goes beyond the financial incentive. It is about recognition for years of representing India and maintaining her sporting association with the state from which she hails.Negi's father, Bhavan Singh Negi, has also questioned the decision, asking whether a daughter ceases to belong to her home state simply because she gets married elsewhere.Speaking from Shillai in Sirmaur district, he pointed out that his daughter had received a cash reward from the Himachal government after the 2023 Asian Games, despite being married in Haryana.That precedent has made the latest omission even harder for the family to comprehend. They believe marriage should not erase an athlete's roots or diminish her contribution to the state she continues to represent in domestic competitions.The controversy has since drawn reactions from political leaders and people associated with sports in Himachal Pradesh.The debate has consequently become about more than a reward announced after a sporting achievement. It has raised questions about how states recognise athletes who continue to bring them distinction despite changes in their personal circumstances.The controversy emerged after Himachal Pradesh Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu announced a cash reward of Rs 1 crore each for three players from the state who were part of India's women's kabaddi gold-medal-winning squad at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.The recipients were Pushpa Rana, Jyoti Thakur and Bhawna Thakur. Indian women's cricket player Renuka Thakur was also announced as a recipient of Rs 1 crore in recognition of her achievements.The announcement followed an earlier disagreement over the amount offered to the kabaddi players. Initially, the three players had been informed that they would receive Rs 33 lakh each, a figure they felt was below their entitlement under the state's sports policy. They subsequently met Sukhu to raise their concerns over the cash incentives and employment opportunities.Pushpa Rana said the players were disappointed by the original announcement."Look, we were very disappointed because according to the sports policy, we were not being given the amount that was due to us. So literally, anyone would be disappointed," she told IANS.Following the meeting, the Chief Minister assured the players that the reward would be increased to Rs 1 crore each. The state government also announced government employment for the three kabaddi players, with options in the police department or the Youth Services and Sports Department.While the revised announcement addressed the players' concerns over the amount, Negi's omission from the list brought a fresh controversy into focus.The Himachal Pradesh government has not publicly provided a definitive explanation for why Negi's name was removed from the list.Sports Minister Yadvinder Goma said he was unaware of the reason behind the change and would examine the file before discussing the matter with the Chief Minister.Meanwhile, sources in the state government indicated that officials were monitoring the Haryana government's position on the matter. They suggested that Himachal Pradesh could consider a decision later, particularly since Haryana had not yet announced a cash award for Negi.The sources also indicated that her employment with Indian Railways was not a factor in the matter.The distinction is important because Negi has maintained that she has continued to represent Himachal Pradesh in domestic competitions despite her marriage and employment outside the state.Whether the government ultimately revises its list remains to be seen. For now, the Sports Minister's assurance that he will review the matter offers a possible route towards resolving the dispute.For Negi, the timing of the controversy is especially poignant.At the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, she captained the women's kabaddi side to gold and received recognition from her home state. At the Aichi-Nagoya Games, she again stood among the Indian players who helped defend the title, contributing to a campaign that ended with another gold medal for the country.Her sporting journey has been built around representing India at the highest level while continuing to identify with Himachal Pradesh. The latest controversy has placed that connection under an uncomfortable spotlight.Negi's case also highlights a broader challenge in Indian sport: ensuring that recognition for athletes reflects their achievements and contributions, rather than becoming entangled in questions about residence, marriage or administrative eligibility.The government has yet to make its final position clear, and the possibility of reconsideration remains open. Until then, the former India captain's disappointment stands as a reminder that recognition can matter as much as the reward itself.

Article Title: EXCLUSIVE | ‘In reality, it really isn’t’: Asian Games gold medallist Pranavi Urs on golf’s ‘rich man’s sport’ image
Article Text:
Gold medallist India's Pranavi Urs celebrates during the women's individual stroke play medal ceremony REUTERS/Andy Chua

Women's golf in India : Pranavi Urs wants more attention

I feel like in this Asian Games, women in sport have done a lot better than the guys. And it just shows that girls don't just sit at home.

Aditi Ashok 's influence and the support behind Pranavi Urs

Gold medallists China's Yan Liu, Zhang Weiwei and Yin Ruoning celebrate during the women's team medal ceremony along with silver medallists India's Pranavi Urs, Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar and bronze medallists Taiwan's Chien Pei-yun, Ya-ni Tseng and Hsu Wei-ling REUTERS/Andy Chua

I didn't grow up playing golf because I wanted fame or money. I play golf because I love the sport. And money and fame is just a bonus.

The triple bogey that tested Pranavi Urs in Nagoya

I did think about Rory because he had a bad start at the Masters when he won it for the first time. And I was like, ‘If he can do it, so can you.’ So, you know, just keep at it. Just stick to your process.

India's Pranavi Urs in action during the women's individual stroke play final REUTERS/Andy Chua

From Asian Games gold to the search for an LET title

"A lot of non-golfers don't know what the sport means or what it is. And they all just think that it's a rich man's sport. In reality, it really isn't."Pranavi Urs, the 23-year-old from Mysuru, has just returned from the Asian Games as the first Indian woman to win an individual golf gold . The medal has changed her place in Indian golf, but she is more interested in what it can do for the sport itself."I think any medal for golf at this point in the golfing world is great for India. So I think any medal, whether it's on the men's side or the women's side, would have brought a lot more attention to the sport, which obviously, at the end of the day, is the goal for us - to give back to the sport and kind of make it global and grow it in India," she told Timesofindia.com from Mysuru."Because I feel like in India, it's definitely picked up in the last few years, but it's not where it should be. And I think getting this gold home, or even the silver, I think is a good step and it's heading in the right direction."That is a bigger ambition than the medal sitting in her collection. And Pranavi sees the women's game as an important part of it. "I think the girls are doing far better than the guys globally. Four or five years ago, there were only one or two girls on the LET (Ladies European Tour), with full status. Now there are five of us."So I think to just go out there and tell everyone and make a statement that the girls are good, and that we're better than the guys, and bring a lot more attention towards women's sports in India; and it doesn't have to be golf."Her own career offers an example of that progress . In December 2025, Pranavi became the first Indian woman to win a professional open-field tournament against male golfers when she won the IGPL Invitational Mumbai. She shot a bogey-free 8-under 60 in the final round and won by two strokes.Pranavi's Asian Games campaign also brought a team silver, with Aditi and Diksha Dagar joining her on the podium in the women's event. Aditi had won individual silver at Hangzhou in 2023, becoming the first Indian golfer to win an Asian Games medal. She was also the first Indian to win on the Ladies European Tour, has five LET titles, has played at three Olympics and finished fourth at Tokyo, one shot off the medals.For Pranavi, Aditi has been a reference point since she was a junior. "Aditi is on a different level. She's my senior. I've looked up to her since I was a little kid, since I was a junior. We have quite similar careers, apart from the fact that I haven't won on the LET yet. She's still the greatest golfer in India."Pranavi's own career began much earlier, at a golf course in Mysuru when she was six. The route since then has taken her through junior golf, the professional ranks and the LET with support around her through all of it."I think I wouldn't have done it without my family. My family has been my biggest support. I've got a really good support system. I have my coach, my S&C coach, my psychologist, my physio. So I've got a really strong base, and I can lean on them whenever I need to. We've got a really good bond. Everyone gets along really well. So I think I've achieved what I've achieved because of my family and my support system."That support is what she points to when asked about the next generation, rather than rankings or prize money. "I just want young girls to pick up a sport, love it, enjoy it, and have fun with it."The money has, nevertheless, become hard to miss after the 2026 Games . Karnataka Govt. announced ₹1 crore for her individual gold and ₹75 lakh for the team silver. The IGPL announced another ₹1 crore for the individual gold, while the Indian Golf Union also announced a reward.For a young golfer looking at what is possible in the sport, Pranavi believes the rewards can be an incentive too. "For someone who thinks like make money or X, Y and Z ... if that motivates them, then sure, so be it. I’m very happy that it's all out there in public for people to see what they can get if they achieve something. So let them be motivated by that. I think each to their own, right? I feel like everybody has a different goal and why they play the sport. "For all the attention that came after the gold, the medal itself was in serious doubt on the third hole of the final round. Pranavi had started the day with a three-shot lead. A triple bogey on the third wiped it out."I think I lost my lead, which was unfortunate, not because of a bad shot, but I just got unlucky on the third. It was out of my control where the ball ended up and what happened."She was one shot behind by the fourth, but her response was not to start chasing every lost shot. "I was like, 'You know what, it's fine. You've hit rock bottom.’ I was one back on the fourth hole. And I was like, ‘You always love chasing. You've already hit rock bottom. Just play fearless and you can do it.'"There was - she remembered - another golfer, a certain Rory McIlroy , who had been in a similar position.The process, she kept coming back to, was simple: stay patient. "There was not a single moment when I didn't think I was not going to win. You just keep doing what you have to do, stick to your process, and just be patient, because it's 18 holes. If I didn't win on the third hole after what happened, that's fine. It's 18 holes."She eventually finished with a 70 for a 15-under 265, one shot clear of China's Yin Ruoning, a former world No. 1 and winner of the 2023 Women's PGA Championship, and Singapore's Shannon Tan, who plays on the Ladies European Tour."All I wanted to do was obviously hole the [final] putt. I don't remember most of it. I was just in the flow. I remember every shot, but I don't remember it as much as I remember the last part, because obviously there are videos and stuff now."And the ability to stay in that flow was something Pranavi learned by spending the last three years playing on the LET, moving between countries, courses and conditions. The travel itself has become part of the job."I think I'm more experienced now because I play in Europe. It's different conditions week in, week out. You've got jet lag, you've got different places, different rooms. You've just got to go with the flow. Just going with the flow and adapting to whatever comes your way - whether it's nervousness or anything - just being able to deal with it and move on."At the 2023 Asian Games, Pranavi finished 13th individually, and the Indian women's team finished fourth. And that is where much of the difference between Hangzhou and Nagoya lies for her. "It's a mental sport. You've got to stay focused, you've got to stay patient.""And, like I said, just kind of preparing yourself week in, week out and travelling around the world, fighting jet lag, fighting being homesick and all of that has helped me grow into a better person and a better golfer." she added.Now, the one thing still missing from her professional record is an LET title. She has had several high finishes in Europe, but no victory yet. “Every golfer has their doubts. If you're not winning, you're like, 'Will I ever win?'", said Pranavi, but Aichi-Nagoya has given her belief that she will eventually win."I beat a world No. 6, so if I can do that, I can win on the LET. Just be patient, keep doing what I'm doing, and eventually I will win. Every golfer goes to win. You give 100%, 200%. That's why golfers go to win. Eventually, I will win."And then there is one small matter of one more first that she wants."An Olympic gold."
Article Summary: Pranavi Urs is the first Indian woman to win an individual golf gold at the Asian Games. The 23-year-old from Mysuru also won silver with Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar. She has five Ladies European Tour titles, has played at three Olympics and finished fourth at Tokyo.

Article Title: Nic Maddinson creates unwanted record for longest duck by a Test opener in 21st century
Article Text:
Australia's Nic Maddinson is bowled on day one of the first cricket test match between South Africa and Australia. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nic Maddinson’s return to Test cricket after nearly a decade got off to a disastrous start as the Australia opener endured a 33-ball duck against South Africa in the first Test at Kingsmead, Durban, on Friday.Maddinson’s 0 off 33 balls is the third-longest duck by an opener in Test history. It is also the longest innings for a duck by a Test opener in the 21st century, making it an unwanted milestone on his comeback to the national side.The 34-year-old was dismissed after Travis Head fell for nine, leaving Australia in early trouble after captain Pat Cummins won the toss and elected to bat on the opening day.Maddinson was drafted into the squad as a replacement for the injured Cameron Green, making a return to the Test set-up after overcoming testicular cancer. His previous Test appearance came during the 2016-17 home summer, when he managed just 27 runs across three matches.However, his recall had come under scrutiny even before the series began, with former Australia opener Matthew Hayden questioning the selectors’ decision to bring back a batter who had not played first-class cricket since early 2025.Speaking on the All Over Bar The Cricket podcast, Hayden launched a scathing attack on the selection panel and questioned the standard of players being picked for the national team.“Where we are at is that we are promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket,” Hayden said.He also questioned the expectation that players with modest first-class averages could translate that form into success at the highest level, taking aim at chief selector George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide.“And if we continue to lay that out and expect that a bloke averaging 35 is going to average 55 in Test match cricket, George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide, you are dreaming. I will just put it that simply. You are frigging dreaming. And you are piling up this dog s*** explanation, and you are, in my opinion, disrespecting first-class cricket. Absolutely dead set you are. You should be picking guys that are averaging 45 or more, and you can’t, because they don’t want to play,” Hayden said.Maddinson’s first-class average of 37.11 had further fuelled the debate around his selection. Cummins, however, had backed the batter ahead of the series, saying he was settled in his game.With Head also dismissed cheaply, Australia faced an early test of their batting depth against a South African side that recalled Anrich Nortje and opted for two spinners. Kagiso Rabada was left out as he continues his recovery from a hamstring injury.
Article Summary: Maddinson's 0 off 33 balls is the third-longest duck by an opener in Test history. It is also the longest innings for a duck by a Test opener in the 21st century. The 34-year-old was dismissed after Travis Head fell for nine, leaving Australia in early trouble.

New Delhi: The Indian cricket board’s ( BCCI ) injury management programme at its Centre of Excellence (CoE) has been under renewed focus over the past 20 months. Now, according to the CoE annual report, accessed by TOI, as many as 32 top men’s team players, including 20 BCCI centrally contracted players and 12 players under a new targeted/India ‘A’ category, underwent rehabilitation for injuries between April 2025 and March 2026. The list has swelled post IPL 2026, with at least two players breaking down in each series.Interestingly, the report states that the BCCI increased the CoE’s budget by nearly Rs 35 crore compared to the actual expenses in the previous financial year. The CoE’s expenses include administrative costs, courses and match expenses.The CoE’s projected expenses for 2026-27 now stand at Rs 127 crore, compared to Rs 92 crore in actual expenses last year.India’s Test and ODI captain Shubman Gill and head coach Gautam Gambhir have been vocal about how difficult it has become to plan tours because of a surge in injuries over the last year. While the report does not specify how many times each player reported to the CoE, it mentions that injuries to 68 players across genders were treated and managed by the BCCI-CoE Sports Science Medicine (SSM) team.When it comes to the nature of the injuries, the majority were soft-tissue injuries.The only impact injury treatment mentioned was that of Rishabh Pant, who underwent treatment following a foot fracture sustained during a Test in Manchester in July 2025.Interestingly, the report also reveals that Rohit Sharma underwent rehabilitation at the CoE during this period, but the BCCI never made an official statement about it. Rohit last reported to the CoE for a hamstring injury following this year’s IPL.The latest Team India players added to the list up to Sept 30 this year are Virat Kohli, Varun Chakravarthy, Prince Yadav and Harsh Dubey, besides multiple ‘targeted’ players. From that list, Jasprit Bumrah, Washington Sundar, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Harshit Rana, Hardik Pandya and Prasidh Krishna have been repeat cases. Rana, Pandya and Reddy have each spent at least four months at the CoE in the last 18 months.The BCCI advertised the post of SSM head at the CoE only last month. The post has been lying vacant since Nitin Patel resigned in March 2025.TOI understands that there has been a breakdown in communication between Team India’s SSM team and the CoE’s SSM team, with cricket head VVS Laxman being the only medium of communication. It has been learnt that Team India strength and conditioning (S&C) coach Adrian Le Roux suggested a few tweaks to workload management routines in June 2025, while the CoE has been reluctant to deviate from its own mechanisms.Personnel from the CoE’s SSM team travelled to domestic tournaments to monitor key India players under the injury prevention and management programme.The last time Indian cricket saw a spate of soft-tissue injuries was in 2021-22, when players suddenly moved out of playing in bubbles during the Covid-19 pandemic. That time, the issue was brought under control in two to three months. In 2017, too, there was a three-month phase when multiple players broke down after S&C coach Shanker Basu introduced drastic changes to the fitness programme.According to the report, 15 of the 57 budgeted camps and tournaments were not conducted in the last audited year.The CoE conducted 25 elite/high-performance camps across age groups and genders, besides special camps for the north-eastern states. It also organised multiple courses and camps for S&C coaches, other coaches and match officials.The CoE started a programme called the ‘training block’ for contracted and targeted/India ‘A’ players. According to the report, 37 players, including 11 contracted players and 26 India ‘A’/targeted players, availed themselves of the programme, which focuses on strength and skill training.
Article Summary: As many as 32 top men’s team players, including 20 BCCI centrally contracted players and 12 players under a new targeted/India ‘A’ category, underwent rehabilitation for injuries between April 2025 and March 2026. The list has swelled post IPL 2026, with at least two players breaking down in each series.

Article Title: India rivals, Indian roots: The stories of Australia ‘A’ stars Nikhil Chaudhary and Tanveer Sangha
Article Text:
Nikhil Chaudhary and Tanveer Sangha (Agency Image)

Puducherry: India are Australia’s biggest on-field rivals. But these days, the Aussies are banking heavily on Indian-origin players who are making a mark at the highest level. As Australia ‘A’ continue their tour of India, two Indian-origin players brought up in different environments, Nikhil Chaudhary and Tanveer Sangha, offer fascinating stories of migration, identity, perseverance and ambition.For Nikhil, Australia was never part of the original plan. Born in Delhi and raised in Ludhiana, he was playing domestic cricket for Punjab when a holiday to Queensland during Covid-19 turned into a life-changing detour.“I was already playing for Punjab. But then I had to make that decision of going away from the family and starting a new journey,” Nikhil told TOI on the eve of Australia’s second ‘A’ one-dayer.The transition meant starting from scratch. He worked at a Mexican restaurant and drove as a courier to pay his bills before cricket began opening doors. The medium-pacer from Punjab eventually reinvented himself as a leg-spinning all-rounder and earned an Australia debut this year.“It’s just a different culture we have in India, where we just take everything for granted because of our mom and dad working hard for us. Here, I had to start from zero. If you are not hard-working and not able to struggle, then it’s not possible to actually play for Australia,” the hard-hitting middle-order batter said.His family in Ludhiana has remained his biggest support system, even though his father’s allegiance during an India-Australia contest remains firmly with the Men in Blue.“My dad still supports India. Just because I moved to Australia doesn’t mean he’s going to support Australia,” Nikhil said.Tanveer, on the other hand, never planned to become a cricketer. Born in Australia to Punjabi parents, he treated cricket as “a little more than a summer pastime”. Leg-spin entered his life around the age of 13 and, slowly, taking wickets began turning a hobby into a possible career.His parents’ journey, however, gave him a deeper appreciation of what it took to reach this level. His father, Joga, who played kabaddi in India and later in Australia, and his mother, Upneet, built their lives as migrants.“They’ve made huge sacrifices to get us here,” Tanveer said. “They’ve given me everything, the resources, their time, taking me everywhere to training and games.”Tanveer is also eyeing a return to the Australian side, with Adam Zampa currently firmly established as the first-choice leg-spinner. The youngster, however, sees Zampa’s presence as motivation rather than a roadblock.“My job is to keep getting better and hopefully take over his spot when he retires,” he said.
Article Summary: Nikhil Chaudhary and Tanveer Sangha offer fascinating stories of migration, identity, perseverance and ambition. For Nikhil, Australia was never part of the original plan. The medium-pacer from Punjab reinvented himself as a leg-spinning all-rounder and earned an Australia debut this year.Tanveer is also eyeing a return to the Australian side.

Article Title: ‘I just like to be the first in everything’: Pranavi Urs sets sights on Olympic medal
Article Text:
Gold medallist India's Pranavi Urs (REUTERS)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bengaluru: Pranavi Urs has always seemed to have a liking for firsts. In 2025, the Mysuru pro became the first Indian woman to win an open-field professional tournament against male golfers when she triumphed at the IGPL Invitational in Mumbai. Last week in Japan, she added the biggest first of them all, becoming the first Indian woman to win an individual gold at the Asian Games.“I just like to be the first in everything,” Pranavi said during an interaction facilitated by SAI. “I find ways to put myself in situations where no one’s ever been before.” For someone who has repeatedly ventured into uncharted territory, the Asian Games gold was another opportunity to test herself.The three-shot lead she carried into the final round disappeared after a triple bogey on the third hole. But unlike three years ago in Hangzhou, Pranavi knew what it was like to be in a high-pressure situation. More importantly, she had prepared for it.The night before the final round, Pranavi and her psychologist had visualised different scenarios, including what could happen if things went wrong. When the triple bogey arrived, she recognised the situation and reminded herself that she had reached rock bottom.“I was like, you’ve got nothing to lose, you’re at rock bottom now. The worst thing has already happened, so it can’t get worse,” she said.That preparation allowed her to return to the process rather than focus on the outcome. Even on the final hole, when the gold was within touching distance, she was thinking about making sure she secured a medal rather than winning it.She changed from a six-iron to a seven-iron for her second shot after feeling the adrenaline rush. She was so locked into the moment that she did not even realise her final putt was for gold.“I thought it was like, make par and maybe force a playoff,” she said. “Little did I know that the last putt that I hit was putt to win.”Hence, there was no elaborate celebration. She did not know she had won. Now, however, the significance of the gold is beginning to sink in, as is the possibility of what it could lead to.Pranavi’s next first could come on the Ladies European Tour, where she has been knocking on the door of a maiden victory. She believes her game is ready and that it is now a matter of patience.“I’ve come close to winning a couple of times. It just shows that my game is there and it’s just a matter of time,” she said.Closer home, the Women’s Indian Open remains a childhood dream. A win on home soil, she feels, would be special in a way no other victory could match.But Pranavi is already looking beyond those targets. Asked what the next ‘first’ she wants to chase is, she said, “To win an Olympic medal or a Major!”For someone who has already broken barriers at the domestic level and the Asian Games, the ambition is clear: the next frontier is no longer India, but the global arenas of the sport.
Article Summary: Pranavi Urs is the first Indian woman to win an individual gold at the Asian Games. She was so locked into the moment that she did not even realise her final putt was for gold. Her next first could come on the Ladies European Tour where she has been knocking on the door of a maiden victory.

Article Title: Between parents' struggles and 'endless coffees': How Savitha Shri became India's only gold medallist at Chess Olympiad | Exclusive
Article Text:

Savitha wins an individual gold on Board 5 at Women's Chess Olympiad (Photo by Michal Walusza for FIDE)

A murky start, and the climb back from Kazakhstan and China

Savitha Shri in Round 10 of Chess Olympiad (Photo by Michal Walusza for FIDE)

The captain who brought the 'endless coffees'

Swayams Mishra at Samarkand Olympiad (FIDE Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What's next?

NEW DELHI: Savitha Shri Baskar emerged as India's golden girl at the 2026 Chess Olympiad, but there was a point when her chess career was funded by her father's gold jewellery, pawned to cover a national tournament's entry fee.Baskar, an electrician in Singapore at the time, would go on to quit that job entirely and move back to India to support her daughter. It was a decision he still calls difficult.The sacrifice, in fact, wasn't only his to make. Chess had first entered the family through Savitha's older brother Mugesh, whom their father had originally set out to build a career around.Savitha's own interest came from watching him play. But once both children were training together, the costs made running two chess careers impossible. Mugesh stepped back after the eighth standard. Savitha kept going.This time, she went to Samarkand as the youngest member of the Indian contingent, brought in after Harika Dronavalli, who felt she'd achieved everything a chess career could offer , including a gold, stepped aside for the next generation.Even then, there were questions about the 19-year-old International Master's spot in the squad. "There were a lot of people who questioned her spot, journalists saying there are players higher than her, and so on," women's captain Swayams Mishra had earlier told TimesofIndia.com "But according to the selection, she was qualified, and she'd won the Asian continental a couple of months ago. She'd also played the World Women's Team Championship, so I knew her as a team player always. Whenever we gave her the opportunity, she delivered. If India won a medal, we owe it to her."Savitha delivered in some style, becoming the only Indian to win an individual gold medal in Uzbekistan, finishing an extraordinary 9/10, and a central figure in India's bronze-medal campaign."Coming to the team as a reserve player, I wasn't even expecting to play all 10 rounds," she told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction. "So I'm grateful for the trust my teammates and my captain had in me, for giving me the opportunity to play all 10. I'm happy with the score, 9 out of 10; but game-wise, I think I could have done a bit better."Around her sat some of the biggest names in Indian women's chess. Looking back at her first experience of the Olympiad, she continued, "It was my first Olympiad, and it has always been a dream for me to play for the country in a tournament like this. We had Humpy (Koneru) akka, who's been the top-most player in women's chess for almost two decades, and we had Vaishali akka and Divya Deshmukh; such a strong team, and we were the first seed in the women's section. I learned a lot from all of them, and Abhijit sir and Swayams sir did a wonderful job with our openings and in every other aspect too. It was a wonderful experience."Despite the individual gold, she's unambiguous about where her priorities sat throughout. "The team medal will always come first, because we're giving out everything for the team. I wasn't even caring about my individual gold; someone told me I'd already secured a medal before the last round, but I only found out I'd won gold after the round finished," she recalled with a laugh. "I was just trying my best to win that last game so we could get a silver as a team. From the position I got, I couldn't really convert anything, but I'm at least happy we got the bronze."The campaign didn't begin smoothly off the board. "When we arrived (in Samarkand) at the hotel, it was around 11:30 at night, and they said they couldn't get the rooms ready," Savitha told this website. "We didn't get our rooms for five or six hours. They made us wait in the lobby, then gave one or two rooms for the whole team."What followed, though, was a federation stepping up as Savitha confirmed, "After that, AICF made sure everything was sorted, and that we got our Indian food every day. The Indian restaurant was so far away that they had to arrange someone to get the delivery done, and they made sure the food was good quality and on time. I don't think any federation would have done that. We're all so grateful for it."On the board, the campaign's defining stretch came against Kazakhstan and China, the two matches where her own result decided India's fate."With both teams, I was the one playing till the last point, and my game was going to be the deciding factor," she said. "It started with Kazakhstan; I got an equal position and was trying to push it. I think what helped me score was time management: after move 40 I was always ahead on the clock compared to my opponent, which put more pressure on them, and I was able to swindle the position."Against China, the margins were just as tight. "It's a bit sad we couldn't win that one," the teenager added. "When I got a better position, Vantika made a blunder at that point and got into a worse position. If she'd been able to hold a draw, I think we'd have got gold fairly easily."Through the toughest stretches, Savitha points to one figure in particular for keeping the team together, especially after an early loss to Poland."Swayams sir is the best captain ever, I think, because of the way he handled our team. We lost to Poland, but he was the one who motivated us. Even during games, if we wanted something, he was always there: water, bananas, everything. For me, he was bringing endless coffees, because I played till the last moment every time. He even jokingly said it was because of those coffees that I was able to swing all my games." The backing went beyond logistics, she said. "He had so much confidence in me. I think he believed in me more than I believed in myself."That trust, she added, was something she'd first experienced a cycle earlier, at the Asian Games, and carried with her into Samarkand."There's just so much you learn from being in a team like that, discussing lines together in team meetings, having those interactions, and them having so much confidence in me. They believed in me more than I did in myself at the time too," she noted.Asked whether she thinks back to what her family gave up to get her here, Savitha is candid, albeit guarded, about letting it weigh on her day-to-day. "If I don't play well, it all comes back to mind. My parents struggled. I know what they've gone through, because they had to spend so much on chess because of me. That's something I'll always remember. But I don't really think much about it while I'm playing, or in general. I just have to stay in the present.Savitha, currently rated 2405, is treating the grandmaster (GM) title as a goal to work toward rather than something owed to her on reputation."The Grandmaster title is definitely my goal, and I'll be working towards it," she said in a confident voice. "I'll be playing tournaments, of course, but for now I think I'll take a bit of rest. The Olympiad is such a big and tiring event. My next tournament will probably be the World Juniors in Namibia, though I might play something before that. I haven't decided yet."On where her game itself needs to sharpen next, she concluded, "In my own game, I think I should get a bit steadier in the openings, and probably work on some positional stuff as well. In the Olympiad, I played the aggressive, complicated positions pretty well; positional chess is the other part I'll be working on."
Article Summary: Savitha Shri Baskar is the only Indian to win an individual gold medal in Uzbekistan. She was brought in after Harika Dronavalli, who felt she'd achieved everything a chess career could offer, stepped aside for the next generation. The 19-year-old International Master was a central figure in India's bronze- medal campaign.

Article Title: ‘We’re not trying to be any other league’: SA20 COO Lynn Naudé on the league’s rapid rise
Article Text:
Lynn Naudé (left), COO of SA20 (Special Arrangement)

Excerpts

SA20 has grown rapidly in four seasons. What has been the biggest lesson behind that success?

How do you keep SA20 distinct in an increasingly crowded global T20 calendar?

What role has the league played in strengthening South African cricket beyond the professional level?

With overseas leagues expanding, how do you ensure SA20 continues attracting elite international players?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Looking ahead to Season 5, what is the one area where you want fans to notice a clear step forward?

NEW DELHI: Four seasons into its existence, SA20 has already established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. But for COO Lynn Naudé, the league’s rapid rise has been less about chasing quick wins and more about getting the fundamentals right. From securing a prime South African summer window and putting Proteas at the heart of the competition to creating a strong match-day atmosphere, Naudé explains how SA20 has built its identity and what lies ahead in Season 5.I think probably the biggest lesson is that strong foundations matter more than quick wins. From the very start, we were very single-minded about what we believed success looked like. The fan experience, the quality of cricket and putting South African players at the heart of the competition were all important to us. We wanted to make sure SA20 felt like it belonged to South African fans as a starting point, and then we could take it global from there.I think that's probably been one of my biggest learnings. If you can get your basics right, the rest will follow from thereT20 cricket has got a unique feeling to it, and that's possibly a common thread. But I think there are a couple of things that have helped us.First, our window and our ability to secure it in the heart of the South African summer, with great conditions and full stadiums, was a real coup for us.That time of year lends itself to delivering a product that speaks very much to the fans, but also provides a fantastic experience both on broadcast and in the stadium.The second is the quality of the competition. The commitment from Cricket South Africa to make all of its Proteas available to play in the tournament season after season, and to see them compete with the best in the world, means that we have intentionally put cricket at the heart of the product.The third is probably the atmosphere at the venues. I think that's become something quite synonymous with SA20.If I had to wrap it up, I'd say we're not trying to be any other league. We're just trying to be the best version of SA20 that we can be.”It has actually been on multiple levels. The intention was for SA20 to almost become a bastion for South African cricket. There was obviously work that needed to be done to strengthen the talent pipeline.But outside of that, if I look back again on the last five seasons, it's also about the quality of the broadcast, what's improved in terms of the fan experience within the South African sporting context, our venues, the ways of working and how they operate on a day-to-day basis.There's also been a lot of knowledge transfer from SA20 into the greater cricket ecosystem, with some of the standards and expectations that we have for the type of product we want to deliver.We've had the opportunity to expose a lot of young talent in the sporting industry to our ways of working and the culture at SA20.In the lead-up to the 2027 World Cup, what we've tried to do is make sure that the cricket ecosystem, and those who deliver not only on the field but also off it, is better off the back of SA20 and the experience it has brought to the South African cricket landscape.At the highest level, elite players want to play where the cricket is competitive, the conditions are good and the environment is professional. I think that's something we strive to offer, and I think we do offer all three.Our franchises bring global experience and know how to run teams. The players know that when they come here, they'll be tested against strong domestic talent and they'll be playing in front of full stadiums.It's always surprising to me, anecdotally, when I hear players talk about how important it is to them to play in front of a crowd and how different it feels. I guess when you're talented like that, you feel appreciated when you're playing in front of a lot of people.That, coupled with the strong and stable franchise ownership groups that we've got, who invest in those players, offers them opportunities.If you have the opportunity to play in the SA20, you also have the opportunity to play in many other places around the world. I think consistency across all of those things will make sure that we remain attractive to players.Every season we run a fan survey, and it directly shapes what we deliver. Our fans have told us what they want to see more of, and they've also told us what they don't want us to change. Those are the types of things that shape our decisions.Our brand positioning at SA20 is ‘for everyone’, and we take that pretty seriously. On the field, it means competitive, world-class cricket for the dedicated cricket fan. Off the field, it really means a great social occasion for people to come and enjoy the atmosphere, the music and a day out with friends and family.If I have to say what I want fans to take away, it's that we do hear you, we do listen to what you want, and we will always strive to deliver based on the feedback that fans are giving us.
Article Summary: Lynn Naudé, COO of SA20, talks to TOI about the league's rapid rise. SA20 has established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. COO says league's success has been down to getting the fundamentals right. He talks about securing a prime South African summer window.

The questions around Sanju Samson 's place in India's T20I side have resurfaced after the wicketkeeper-batter endured another modest outing in the series opener against the West Indies, but former India opener Aakash Chopra believes dropping him for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is not an option at this stage.Samson has managed scores of 11, 2, 7 and 9 in his last four T20I innings, including a five-over contest against Japan. The recent run has come after he struck back-to-back fifties in the T20I series against Afghanistan.However, Sooryavanshi's emergence has added another dimension to the selection debate. The teenage batter opened alongside Abhishek Sharma during the Asian Games, with Samson batting at No. 3. VVS Laxman was India's head coach for the tournament, with Gautam Gambhir occupied with the ODI team against the West Indies.For the ongoing series, India have returned to the opening combination of Samson and Abhishek, the pair that featured in the team's T20 World Cup-winning campaign. Samson, however, managed only nine in the first T20I against the West Indies in Lucknow.Chopra has backed the Kerala batter to retain his place, arguing that the team cannot keep questioning his position after every failure.Speaking in a video shared on his YouTube channel, 'Aakash Chopra,' the former India opener dismissed the prospect of Sooryavanshi replacing Samson for the second T20I."Since Bihar is in the neighborhood, there is talk of Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Will there be a chance of him playing? No, it won't be there. You will have to agree that it cannot happen that he plays now, and if we start saying this about Sanju Samson after every match, then we are damned. How will you manage cricket then? Just don't go there," he said.Chopra also discussed the possibility of India bringing Nitish Kumar Reddy into the playing XI, admitting that he would like to see the all-rounder given a chance but was unsure whether the team management shared that view."I seriously think about Nitish Kumar Reddy for sure. However, I can't do that either after the first match. I wanted you to play Nitish from the start itself, because how will you prepare him? However, that's my thinking and might be your thinking as well, but the Indian team is not thinking like that," he observed.India head into the second T20I in Ranchi on Friday, October 9, with a 1-0 lead in the five-match series after securing an emphatic eight-wicket victory in Lucknow.For Samson, the immediate task is to turn his start into a substantial contribution and quieten the growing criticism. He was dropped after three failures during India's tour of the UK, having been named Player of the Tournament at the T20 World Cup.With Sooryavanshi continuing to attract attention, Samson will be keen to make the most of his opportunity. While Chopra has played down the prospect of an immediate change, the debate over India's opening combination is unlikely to disappear if the wicketkeeper-batter's struggles continue.
Article Summary: Aakash Chopra says Sanju Samson should not be dropped from India's T20I side. The wicketkeeper-batter endured another modest outing in the series opener against the West Indies. Chopra believes dropping Samson for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is not an option at this stage.

Article Title: 'Our cameras will be sharp': South African broadcaster SuperSport takes a dig at Australia over Sandpapergate ahead of Test series

South African sports broadcaster SuperSport has taken a dig at Australia ahead of their first Test series in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, also known as Sandpapergate. Australia will face South Africa in a three-match series, with the opening Test scheduled at Kingsmead in Durban on Friday, October 9, at 1 pm IST.SuperSport posted a promo on X ahead of the three-Test series, saying its cameras “will be sharp”. The post included a camera emoji, bringing back memories of the incident at Newlands in Cape Town in 2018.SuperSport's reference goes back to March 24, 2018, when its cameras caught Australian batter Cameron Bancroft working on the ball with a small yellow object during a Test against South Africa at Newlands.The footage showed Bancroft using the object on the ball before putting it down his trousers. The incident led to the ball-tampering scandal that came to be known as Sandpapergate.The footage was shown on the big screen at the ground. Australia's then head coach Darren Lehmann sent a message to 12th man Peter Handscomb, while the incident quickly became a major talking point in cricket.SuperSport's cameras had also been asked to look out for anything unusual during the series after the umpires reportedly became suspicious about Australia's efforts to alter the ball.The broadcaster's coverage included more than 30 cameras, with 18 operated by camera crews.Australia's current squad includes several players who were part of the team during the Newlands scandal.Steve Smith, who was Australia's captain at the time, is now vice-captain under Pat Cummins. Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon also played at Newlands in 2018. Matthew Renshaw, who joined the squad as a replacement for the final Test of that series, is also back in the team.David Warner has retired, while Cameron Bancroft has not played a Test for more than six years.The scandal has received more attention in the Australian media than in South Africa in recent weeks. However, the team could still face some reminders of the incident during the tour.South Africa enter the series as reigning World Test Championship winners after beating Australia in last year's final at Lord's. Australia, meanwhile, will look to collect points in the 2025-27 World Test Championship cycle. The second Test will be played in Gqeberha from October 18.The third Test, scheduled to begin at Newlands on October 27, will bring Australia back to the venue where the 2018 scandal unfolded.
Article Summary: SuperSport posted a promo on X ahead of the three-Test series. It included a camera emoji, bringing back memories of the incident at Newlands in Cape Town in 2018. Australia will face South Africa in a three-match series, with the opening Test scheduled at Kingsmead in Durban on Friday, October 9.

Ranchi: Nearly four years after his last international appearance at the JSCA International Cricket Stadium, Ishan Kishan returns to familiar territory on Friday when India take on the West Indies in the second T20I, carrying the form and confidence of a player who has fought his way back into the Indian team.Ishan’s last international game here came in January 2023, when India lost a T20I to New Zealand. Much has changed since then. He subsequently lost his place in the India set-up, was dropped from the BCCI central contract list and then embarked on a comeback that has eventually seen him become an integral part of the national side.Now, with good form behind him and his home crowd in front of him, Kishan has a chance to turn his long-awaited return to Ranchi into a memorable one. The timing could hardly be better. India made a statement in the opening T20I, chasing down West Indies’ 172 in just 14 overs. Their aggressive approach left the visitors’ bowling attack with little room for error, and Kishan will be keen to make his own contribution as India look to take a 2-0 lead.India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak said the change of venue would not alter the team’s philosophy. “The way we are approaching the game, with a fearless approach and putting the team first, that’s the same way we will go,” Kotak said ahead of the game here on Thursday.Yet Ranchi could demand a little more adaptability than the opening game did.Though Kotak said on the eve of the match that “the pitch looked a good batting track”, the venue has not traditionally been a high-scoring T20 ground. In four T20Is here, the 200-run mark has never been breached, with India’s 196 for six against Sri Lanka in 2016 remaining the highest score. New Zealand have also successfully defended 176 at the venue.Rain and cool, cloudy conditions could add another variable, while dew may become important later in the evening. With temperatures expected to hover between 22°C and 24°C during match time, India could have to balance their attack carefully, particularly if they end up bowling second.That brings another selection question. Mayank Yadav was expensive in the opening game, leaving India to consider whether to persist with the express quick or bring fit-again Prince Yadav into the attack. They also have considerable spin depth, with Axar Patel, Kuldeep Yadav, Ravi Bishnoi and debutant Naman Dhir among the options. But if dew sets in, India’s spinners could find their task considerably harder.There is also a growing selection subplot in the batting department. The presence of teenage prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has increased the pressure on Sanju Samson , who has struggled for runs in his last four T20Is, scoring 11, 2, 7 and 9. With the teenager waiting in the wings, another low score could make the competition for the Kerala wicketkeeper-batter’s spot more interesting.West Indies, meanwhile, need a vastly improved bowling effort. Bowling coach Ravi Rampal admitted that his young attack, with most of its members having fewer than 15 or 20 T20I appearances, failed to maintain its execution for long enough in the opener.“It just boils down to the experience of the bowling group and then the execution of our plans. We weren’t good enough to execute for a longer period during the game,” Rampal said.That execution will be tested again by an Indian batting line-up that showed little hesitation in taking on the bowlers from the outset.But amid all the tactical questions, Ranchi’s biggest storyline remains Kishan. His journey back to India has already been significant. A substantial innings at the ground where his international journey briefly stalled would add another satisfying chapter to his comeback story.For Kishan, Friday is more than another T20I. It is a homecoming, and an opportunity to make it count.
Article Summary: India take on West Indies in second T20I at JSCA International Cricket Stadium. Ishan Kishan returns to his home ground for first time since January 2023. India made a statement in opening game, chasing down 172 in just 14 overs.

Article Title: 'Tell your story': Pat Cummins' blunt response to Usman Khawaja's book on Sandpapergate

Cummins says the team has moved on

Khawaja’s book could revisit the scandal

Broadcaster takes a dig at Australia

Australia captain Pat Cummins has played down concerns that Usman Khawaja ’s upcoming autobiography could bring fresh attention to the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, also known as Sandpapergate.Australia are returning to South Africa for the first time since the scandal. The three-Test series begins at Kingsmead on Friday, but Cummins said the incident had already been dealt with and the team had moved on.Cummins was part of the Australian bowling attack during the Test against South Africa in Cape Town in March 2018. Australia were caught using sandpaper to rough up one side of the ball illegally to generate more swing.The scandal created a major crisis for Cricket Australia. Captain Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft, who was caught with sandpaper in his pocket, were banned for their roles in the incident.Cummins and fellow bowlers Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon denied knowing about the ball-tampering.All four are now back in South Africa for the three-Test series.Cummins confirmed that he had spoken to Khawaja, who was also part of the Australian team during the 2018 Test at Newlands. However, he said they did not discuss the matter in detail.“Didn't go back into too much detail. He just basically gave me the heads-up that he's doing a book, and yeah, as always, no worries.Tell your story. It's fine,” Cummins said.Australian media reports have said that Khawaja had wanted the entire team to accept collective responsibility after the scandal. However, the suggestion was reportedly rejected at the time.Cummins said he did not know what Khawaja had written in his autobiography, which is due to be published next month.“You need to ask him,” he said. “It’s obviously a long time ago. All the investigations, everything was done back then. Answered every question a million times. So, yeah, it was dealt with then. Now all I can say is, as a group, we moved on, very happy with the last eight years, how we’ve been as a group and evolved.”South African broadcaster SuperSport, whose cameras captured the ball-tampering incident in 2018, has also brought the episode back into focus.The broadcaster shared a social media clip showing Bancroft using sandpaper on the ball and the Australian team’s reaction after the players were caught.SuperSport added a warning ahead of the upcoming series, saying: “Our cameras will be sharp for this 3-match test series.”

The Pakistan Super League is heading for another scheduling collision with the Indian Premier League . The Pakistan Cricket Board on Thursday confirmed that PSL 12 will begin on March 18, 2027, and run until May 2, putting the tournament on a potential collision course with IPL 2027 for the second successive season.The eight-team PSL, which expanded from six teams this year, will retain its current format, with the final scheduled for May 2. While the IPL 2027 schedule is yet to be officially announced, indications are that its 20th season could also begin around the middle of March, raising the prospect of the two major T20 leagues once again competing for players, viewers and global attention.The scheduling overlap could once again create headaches for both leagues, with the IPL also looking at an earlier start in 2027. IPL Governing Council chairman Arun Dhumal had previously indicated that the BCCI was exploring an early-March start, with the aim of completing the tournament by mid-May.“This year, IPL started around March 29 [28], and it was over by May 31,” Saikia told PTI. “Only thing which we are discussing is that during the fag end of the tournament after May 15... there is apprehension of having rainfall or pre-monsoon season starting.On the other hand, there is hot weather which is not very conducive either for the players or for the crowds.“So therefore, there is a discussion going on in BCCI as well as in our IPL governing council regarding whether we can start the tournament a little bit earlier than the fag end of March.“From next year, we will make an effort and I have already instructed our general manager (games development) [former India fast bowler Abey Kuruvilla] to look for the windows, whether we can start it by 10th of March and conclude it by 15th of May. So that there are no adverse weather conditions in the run-up to the playoffs and the finals of IPL 2027, which will be the 20th edition,'' Saikia added.The scheduling overlap could prove particularly significant after the events of the previous season, when several overseas players withdrew from PSL commitments before joining IPL franchises as replacements.Among them was Australian pacer Spencer Johnson, who had been signed directly by Quetta Gladiators before pulling out, citing personal reasons, and subsequently joining Chennai Super Kings as a replacement for Nathan Ellis.Sri Lanka's Dasun Shanaka, who had been signed by Lahore Qalandars, also joined Rajasthan Royals as a replacement, while Zimbabwe pacer Blessing Muzarabani withdrew from his Islamabad United contract to join Kolkata Knight Riders. Muzarabani was subsequently handed a two-year ban from the PSL.The March 18-May 2 window was finalised following consultations with the franchises and other stakeholders during the PSL Governing Council meeting in London on September 1. The PSL will enter its second season with eight teams, after Hyderabad Kingsmen and the expansion of the competition in 2026. The previous season also marked another major shift, with the traditional player draft replaced by an auction for the first time.Peshawar Zalmi ended a nine-year wait for the PSL title in 2026, defeating debutants Hyderabad Kingsmen in the final at Gaddafi Stadium. The match attracted a record crowd of 32,461.PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi said the league would look to build on the momentum generated by the previous season.“PSL 11 showed the world what this league is capable of, thrilling moments that had the whole nation transfixed, record crowds, record broadcasts,” Naqvi said.“PSL 12 will raise the bar further. We are committed to delivering another outstanding season and look forward to seeing all eight franchises compete once again for the title,” he added.
Article Summary: PSL 12 will begin on March 18, 2027, and run until May 2. The eight-team PSL, which expanded from six teams this year, will retain its current format. The IPL 2027 schedule is yet to be officially announced, but indications are that its 20th season could also begin around the middle of March.

Article Title: ‘I’m not going to the military’: What is military exemption? Why South Korea weighs cuts after Asian Games backlash
Article Text:
South Korean football team after winning the Asian Games gold medal. (Pic credit: X)

What is South Korea's military exemption for athletes?

Why is South Korea considering cuts now?

History of the athlete exemption

Who else benefited at the Asian Games?

Will South Korea abolish military exemptions for athletes?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

South Korea is reconsidering a decades-old military service benefit for elite athletes after controversial comments by Asian Games gold medallists triggered a fresh public debate over whether sporting success should continue to qualify some young men for an alternative to the country's compulsory military service.The controversy erupted after South Korea won the men's football gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, beating Japan 1-0 in the final on Saturday. Several players came under fire for comments and social-media activity related to the military benefit that came with their gold medal.Captain Lee Gi-hyuk, winger Yang Min-hyuk and forward Park Seung-soo all faced criticism. Lee held up his gold medal and said, “I’m not going to the military,” while Yang said the military-service benefit had been his main motivation during the tournament. Park posted a photograph of himself wearing a cap associated with people who have completed their mandatory military service.All three subsequently apologised. But the episode reignited a much bigger question in South Korea: why should athletes receive special treatment when most young men are required to serve?The government is now reviewing the system.Culture, Sports and Tourism Minister Chae Hwi-young said Wednesday that his ministry would consult the sports and arts communities, the Defence Ministry and the Military Manpower Administration as it considers comprehensive measures.The Defence Ministry has gone further. It said it was considering either scaling back or abolishing supplementary military service for artists and athletes, while Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said the ministry's goal was to gradually reduce the exemptions and ultimately abolish them.South Korea has a mandatory military-service system under which able-bodied men generally have to complete between 18 and 21 months of service.But athletes who achieve specified international sporting results can receive an alternative-service benefit instead of serving the standard term. Under the current rules, athletes who win an Olympic medal or an Asian Games gold medal qualify for the arrangement.The term “military exemption” is widely used, but it can be slightly misleading.The athletes are not simply released from every military-related obligation. Those who qualify are assigned to supplementary service. They undergo three weeks of basic military training and then have to complete 544 hours of community service over 34 months.For elite athletes, however, the difference is significant.Instead of spending 18 to 21 months in regular military service, they can continue training and competing while completing their alternative-service obligations. That can be particularly important for footballers, golfers, baseball players and other professionals whose careers can be affected by a long interruption during their peak years.The benefit can also have implications for athletes playing overseas because avoiding a lengthy interruption can allow them to maintain their club careers and development.At the 2026 Asian Games, 20 of South Korea's 23 men's football players became eligible for the benefit after the 1-0 victory over Japan.The immediate trigger is the backlash over the footballers' comments.Yang Min-hyuk was criticised after saying the medal and championship were not important to him and that he had played with the military-service benefit in mind.Lee's “I’m not going to the military” remark also drew criticism, while Park's photograph wearing a military discharge-style cap became another focus of the controversy.The players later apologised, with Lee saying he should have considered the weight of his words and Yang explaining that the military benefit was one of several motivations that had been expressed poorly.But the government response suggests the controversy is being viewed as part of a wider problem rather than as an isolated incident.The Defence Ministry said it would consider fairness among people subject to mandatory service, the declining number of people available for military service and public consensus when deciding the future of the supplementary-service system.South Korea's declining birth rate means the pool of young men available for military service is shrinking. That demographic pressure has added importance to the question of who can receive alternative arrangements.There is also a fairness argument. While athletes can qualify through sporting achievements, other high-profile South Koreans have had to complete military service.The issue has been particularly sensitive in the entertainment industry because members of BTS, one of South Korea's biggest cultural exports, completed their military obligations rather than receiving an athlete-style exemption.The comparison has repeatedly featured in the debate over whether exceptional achievements in sport, popular culture or other fields should qualify someone for special treatment.The system dates back to 1973, when South Korea introduced the special arrangement for athletes and artists as part of a broader effort to develop elite talent and enhance the country's international standing.Over the decades, the policy became particularly important in sports such as football and baseball, where military service could interrupt the careers of players competing at home and overseas.The Asian Games has traditionally been especially significant because gold, rather than simply any medal, is required for athletes to qualify.That has sometimes produced unusual incentives around the tournament. For South Korea's football and baseball players, an Asian Games gold medal can effectively remove the possibility of a lengthy interruption to their professional careers.The policy has also generated controversy before.Debates intensified after South Korea's run to the 2002 World Cup semi-finals led to a special exemption arrangement for members of that squad, although the World Cup was later removed from the exemption rules.The system has continued to face questions over whether sporting achievement should be sufficient grounds for an alternative to compulsory service.The football players were not the only South Koreans to qualify.South Korea's baseball players earned the benefit after defeating Japan 3-1 in the final. Gold medallists in esports also qualified under the rules.Golfer Tom Kim won the men's individual gold after travelling to Japan following the Presidents Cup. His response to the military-service issue was markedly different from the comments that triggered the controversy.“I’m more proud that I’m able to bring a medal for my country,” Kim said.The episode therefore illustrates the two sides of the current debate: the argument that sporting success can justify an alternative service arrangement for athletes representing South Korea, and the growing concern that such benefits may be difficult to reconcile with the principle that military service should be shared fairly.There is no immediate abolition, but the government is now openly discussing major changes.The Defence Ministry said it plans to reflect a reduction or abolition of supplementary service for artists and athletes in its defence-reform plans. Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul subsequently said the ministry's goal was to gradually scale back the system and ultimately abolish it.The Culture Ministry is separately reviewing the system and plans to consult athletes, artists, defence officials and the Military Manpower Administration before deciding on comprehensive measures.That means the controversy surrounding the Asian Games footballers could have consequences well beyond their apologies.A system that has existed for more than five decades is now facing a renewed examination at a time when South Korea is dealing with a shrinking pool of young men available for military service and changing public expectations about fairness.For athletes, the debate is ultimately about more than a medal. An Asian Games gold can currently mean the difference between an 18-to-21-month interruption and a much less disruptive alternative-service arrangement.For the government, the question is whether that distinction remains justified — and whether a benefit created more than 50 years ago still fits the realities of modern South Korea.
Article Summary: South Korea is reconsidering a decades-old military service benefit for elite athletes. Controversy erupted after South Korea won the men's football gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, beating Japan 1-0 in the final on Saturday. Several players came under fire for comments and social-media activity related to the military benefit.
